subject: Accounting
title: The Fraud Triangle
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Fraud Triangle usable.

hook.text: Why do honest people commit fraud? Criminologist Donald Cressey found three ingredients are needed.

buildup.text: The fraud triangle has three sides: pressure, opportunity, and rationalization.

discovery.text: Pressure is the motive—debt, lifestyle, or gambling. Opportunity is weak controls. Rationalization is the excuse.

twist.text: Remove any one side and fraud becomes much less likely. Strong internal controls cut opportunity.

climax.text: Forensic accountants study the triangle to predict where fraud is most likely to occur.

punchline.text: Pressure plus opportunity plus excuses equals fraud.

quiz.question: What are the three elements of the fraud triangle?

details.summary: The fraud triangle explains the three conditions that are typically present when fraud occurs: pressure (motivation), opportunity (ability), and rationalization (justification). This topic covers each element and how understanding them helps prevent and detect fraud.
details.whyItMatters: The fraud triangle is the most widely used framework for understanding why people commit fraud. Every anti-fraud program should address all three elements to be effective.
takeaways: Pressure is the financial or personal motivation driving someone to commit fraud
Opportunity exists when internal controls are weak enough to allow fraud to occur undetected
Rationalization is the mental justification that allows otherwise honest people to cross ethical lines

faq.question: What is the fraud triangle?
faq.answer: Developed by criminologist Donald Cressey, the fraud triangle identifies three factors typically present in fraud: pressure (financial need or personal motivation), opportunity (weak controls that enable fraud), and rationalization (the mindset that justifies the act). All three usually coexist.

faq.question: How does the fraud triangle help prevent fraud?
faq.answer: Organizations can reduce opportunity through strong internal controls, minimize pressure through employee assistance programs and fair compensation, and address rationalization through ethics training and a strong ethical culture. Eliminating any one element can prevent fraud.
